title: The Pharaoh's Xylophone
paragraphs: One summer, a happy little girl named Mia lived in a yellow house with her family. Her mother baked bread in the kitchen, and her sister grew one giant flower in the garden, an orange and purple flower taller than the window. Mia's friend Sam came from school every night for dinner because he loved her mother's cookie.

Yesterday, a weird package arrived at the address of their neighbor, Mr. Okafor, who ran a small business in the village at the foot of a mountain. He could not remember ordering anything, so he wondered whether it was a mistake. He carried it to the library, where his daughter worked, and asked Mia and Sam to help.

The daughter was a calm character with great knowledge of every language, and her favorite question was always "Why?" She opened the package immediately. Inside, buried in a miscellaneous pile of old paraphernalia, was a xylophone said to belong to a pharaoh, along with a long questionnaire about how the buyer planned to use it. Beside it lay a piece of jewelry shaped like a key.

A note said, "I recommend you keep this safe. You will receive the rest on a beautiful occasion tomorrow." "It is definitely meant for someone else," said Mr. Okafor, "and I would not want to embarrass anyone by guessing who." The daughter pointed at the wall. "The government office keeps a calendar," she said. "We can check the schedule and separate the real events from the fake ones."

By then the winter wind was rattling the library window, so Mia put a cookie in her pocket and picked up her pencil. "Do you ever wonder what is out there?" she asked, and she drew a rocket on the back of the note. It was a simple drawing, but when she touched it with her finger, the clock on the wall stopped, and the paper began to shine. Soon a real rocket stood on the ground outside, round and bright like a button.

Mia's little sister ran in from the garden and begged to come along. So the three of them climbed aboard with the daughter, pressed the big number seven, and flew away from Earth toward a new planet, while the xylophone rang softly in Mia's bag.

They landed on an island in a thick jungle. A monkey swung from a tree, a rabbit hopped past, and a zebra drank water from a river. "Every animal here is so friendly," said Sam, and they began to laugh. The daughter looked around at the quiet environment. "I can hardly believe it," she said.

A tiger stepped out of the shadow of a tree. "Listen," the tiger said, "the queen wants to meet you." A dragon carried them over a bridge to a busy market full of cheerful people, where the queen was waiting with a big smile.

The queen, who was also an entrepreneur and a connoisseur of rare instruments, led them to a cemetery at the edge of the market for a rendezvous with her lieutenant. He was a conscientious man with a heavy conscience, and he worked as the liaison between her palace and the guards. Her chauffeur waited nearby with a golden cart.

"The xylophone is only a minuscule part of a much larger dilemma," the lieutenant warned. Fluorescent lights flickered in the old hall, and a silhouette moved behind the curtain. "Surveillance cameras are ubiquitous here, yet none of them caught the thief. It is a strange phenomenon, and a mischievous one."

When Mia struck the first bar, the xylophone made a sound like onomatopoeia come alive: ping, plink, plonk. The rhythm was hypnotic. Someone had scratched a mnemonic into the wood to help a player remember the order of the notes, and the idiosyncrasy of the instrument was that every note was out of tune on purpose.

Their reconnaissance of the basement revealed an old threshold, and behind it lay the ruins of a tyranny: a hierarchy of officials who loved bureaucracy and hypocrisy more than the truth. Members of the bourgeoisie had once tried to supersede the pharaoh's law, and their sacrilegious plan had left behind only a lust for vengeance.

They crept through a tunnel, and the temperature dropped with every step. At the end, they stopped to rest at a tiny restaurant at the foot of a tall tower, where the cook told them an interesting story. There had been an argument at the last palace meeting, he said, though it was only about the grammar on a sign.

The tower was of great height, and its twin ran parallel to it at the opposite end of the courtyard. It took real strength to climb the stairs. "Maintenance of the tower is necessary every spring," said the lieutenant, "and it is good exercise for the guards. Last year we even brought a vacuum to clean the dust."

Then one of the guards caught pneumonia, and the doctor ordered a quarantine. The others had to maneuver carefully around the sickroom, but their perseverance never faded, and no occurrence of bad luck could break their camaraderie. A professor of psychology joined them to study the case, and after a long meeting the vote to indict the thief was unanimous. Even the thief chose to acquiesce.

At the top of the tower, the key opened a little door. Inside they found a surprise: the thief's hiding place, and a letter that explained everything. It was a guarantee that the xylophone would never be taken again. "What a success," said the daughter, "and how relevant a message can be, even when it comes by such an unusual path!"

The old tools were now obsolete, and the sound of the xylophone was only ephemeral, fading like a dream. The queen agreed to accommodate the instrument in a glass case, and a gauge on the wall kept the air perfectly dry. When the party began to finish, Mia hugged the queen, climbed back into the rocket, and flew home to her mother, happy.
